title: KV prefetch timing spectra and bank-latency rootcause journal
content:
Purpose and short summary:
This is a lab-journal tracking an investigation into intermittent tail-latency spikes correlated with KV cache miss storms. Hypothesis refined over several experiments: not all miss storms are pure capacity/eviction effects — a significant fraction is due to poor alignment of prefetch timing with DRAM bank service windows, causing queuing and effective bandwidth collapse for hotpage groups.

Background / why this started:
- Product incident on 2024-08-29: 99.9th latency increased by ~3x for a customer mix dominated by many short chat sessions (seqlen 32–128).
- Initial telemetry showed large KB-sized read bursts to KV store and NVMe paging was not the dominant latency source. Memory bandwidth counters and DRAM queue depth hinted at bank queuing.

What we measured (setup):
- Cluster: 4x p4d-ish test nodes (A100/80GB equivalent venv), 128GB host DRAM, PCIe NVMe as backing store.
- Runtime build: branch pref-pipeline-experiments (PR linked above).
- Workload: mix of chat workloads (70% short convo: seqlen 32–64, 30% mid: 128–256) replayed from production traces (sampled).
- Cache config: KV cache resident target 40GB, eviction LRU variants tested, prefetch: enabled sync prefetch on read miss with N=2 lookahead, async prefetch window 0–8ms tunable.
- Measurement tools: perf, Nsight microbenchmarks, hwloc sampling, custom evict/reuse tracer instrumented into runtime (trace id -> per-request reuse score).

Key metrics we tracked per experiment:
- reuse_rate: fraction of requests resolved from KV cache without spillback (0.0–1.0)
- eviction_rate: pages evicted per second (pages/s)
- avg_dram_bandwidth (GiB/s)
- bank_util_spread: stddev across DRAM bank service counters (higher implies skew)
- tail_lat_95 and tail_lat_99 (ms) for token generation pipeline end-to-end

Experiment log (chronological):
1) 2024-09-12: baseline reproduction- baseline config reproduced 99.9 spike. Metrics: reuse_rate 0.62, eviction_rate 420 pages/s, avg_dram_bandwidth 48 GiB/s, bank_util_spread 0.18, tail_lat_99 = 420ms (baseline ~150ms). Observed periodic bursts at 200–400ms intervals.

2) 2024-09-14: turn off prefetch entirely- hypothesis: prefetch storms amplify bank contention.- Observed: reuse_rate dropped to 0.56 (expected), eviction_rate increased 22% (more synchronous misses), avg_dram_bandwidth dropped to 37 GiB/s, bank_util_spread 0.07 (more even but low), tail_lat_99 improved to 320ms (partial). Interpretation: prefetch helped reuse but sometimes aligns poorly causing short intense bursts that cause queuing; turning it off trades burstiness for lower overall bandwidth.

3) 2024-09-18: add jitter to prefetch timing (random ±2ms), async queue depth cap 4- Observed: reuse_rate ~0.60, eviction_rate 380 pages/s, avg_dram_bandwidth 44 GiB/s, bank_util_spread 0.11, tail_lat_99 = 210ms. Jitter reduced synchronized bursts and improved tail.

4) 2024-09-22: bank-aware prefetch steering (prototype): map prefetch targets to bank-round-robin order to avoid hot bank concentration- Implementation: cheap hash on page addr -> bank_slot, stagger start times by bank_slot * 200us.- Observed: reuse_rate 0.61, eviction_rate 365 pages/s, avg_dram_bandwidth 46 GiB/s, bank_util_spread 0.04 (much more even), tail_lat_99 = 180ms.

5) 2024-09-25: simulate pathological stride that collides to same bank (worst-case stride 4P pages)- Without steering: bank_util_spread 0.36, tail_lat_99 510ms. With steering: bank_util_spread 0.06, tail_lat_99 190ms. Conclusion: bank-aware staggering greatly reduces worst-case queuing.

6) 2024-09-30: eviction policy variant A/B (age-first vs access-frequency hybrid) with bank steering enabled- age-first gave slightly lower eviction_rate but slightly worse reuse_rate on bursty patterns; hybrid performed best overall for sustained mixed workload. Tail differences minor (hybrid better by ~10–15ms at p99).

Micro-observations / traces:
- Trace sample ID 20240912-TR-22: saw sequence of 14 prefetch requests within 1.2ms converging on same channel/bank -> CPU saw queue length spike, PCIe completion burst delayed -> few requests hit runtime stall path waiting on KV page -> token generation pipeline stalled for >200ms.
- Perf counters show sustained increase in DRAM row-buffer conflicts during these bursts (row activations per ms spiked).

Hypotheses formed:
- Synchronized prefetch wakes (many in-flight prefetches with near-identical timing) are primary driver of bank queuing, especially under high short-session concurrency.
- Capacity/eviction interacts: when reuse_rate is marginal (~0.6), small timing differences push load from amortized background to synchronous critical path.
- NVMe spillback still matters for extreme cache pressure but is orthogonal for the typical mid-range spikes we observed.

Actionable changes prototyped (and next steps):
1) Bank-aware prefetch staggering (prototype above) looks promising — needs refinement for mapping across NUMA nodes. Follow-up: instrument mapping correctness on multi-socket tests (EPIC-1091).
2) Prefetch jitter as a simple mitigation is low-risk and can be rolled quickly behind a feature flag. Consider default jitter = 0.5–2ms depending on concurrency.
3) Add adaptive prefetch window based on observed bank_util_spread: when spread > 0.15, reduce lookahead and insert extra jitter.
4) Improve trace correlation between runtime trace ids and hw counters — currently manual. Build small shim to export per-request bank_assignment and prefetch timestamps to analytics.
5) Add unit tests / microbench harness that synthesizes worst-case strides and verifies bank steering reduces spread below 0.08 at 95% confidence.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How steering interacts with persistent page layout (OS-level page allocator behavior): if physical pages change after migration, bank mapping might not be stable. Need to check consistency across cgroup restarts and hugepage use.
- Is the added latency from staggering an issue at extremely low-latency workloads? (We saw no regression at median but must validate for sub-50ms SLOs.)- Does steering introduce adversarial patterns where an attacker can craft requests to overload a subset of banks? Likely low risk but call out for threat modeling.

Notes on instrumentation and artifacts:
- repo PR: serving-runtime/prefetch-steering-proto (see linked PR).
- profiler snippets saved in /artifacts/lab/2024-09-prefetch-steer/ (internal storage).
- small reproducible harness added: tools/kv-bankbench (script: kv-bankbench --stride=4 --concurrency=256 --duration=300s).

Suggested immediate timeline:
- Short term (1 week): ship jitter behind flag + enable steering behind experimental flag to a small fleet. Run A/B on canary to collect metrics.- Medium (2–4 weeks): refine bank steering to handle NUMA and hugepages; add analytics export; add microbench regression tests.
- Longer (quarter): consider integrating adaptive prefetch controller that uses live bank/util telemetry to tune lookahead and prefetch sequencing automatically.

Appendix: quick commands run during experiments:
- run harness: ./tools/kv-bankbench --trace sample-trace-09 --concurrency 128 --prefetch=on --jitter=0.0- perf counters (example): perf stat -a -e r8151,cycles,instructions -I 1000 ./bin/serving-runtime --load config.yaml- bank spread snapshot: (from custom hwprobe) BankCounts = [1203, 1188, 1197, 1210, 1194, 1180, 1220, 1208], stddev=13 -> normalized 0.04.

TL;DR: prefetch timing alignment was amplifying bank contention causing tail spikes. Two pragmatic mitigations — light jitter and bank-aware staggering — materially reduce tail latencies while preserving most of the prefetch benefit. Next: validate across NUMA and production canary, wire up observability to detect recurrence automatically.

Authors / contact: Aisha Gupta (owner) — please ping on #eng-serving-runtime or DM on Slack for quick sync.
